title: How Much Claude Code Costs for an Engineering Team
summary: What a 30-person engineering team pays for Claude Code on seats, the API and Enterprise, with measured costs per model and per session, and where to set spend limits.
body_markdown:
According to Anthropic, engineering teams spend[$150 to $250 per developer per month](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/costs) on average for Claude Code. However, that's not necessarily how much you'll actually pay, because there are two types of pricing: API rates and subscriptions.


On subscriptions, you get more usage than you would get paying the same amount in API-rate pricing.


For example, I have a personal $200 Claude Ultra subscription. Last month, this subscription allowed me to use $4,988 worth of tokens at API pricing. You get to see this by running` /usage` in an active Claude Code session. Subscriptions are heavily subsidized as a customer acquisition and market-share strategy.


Intuitively, you could budget $200 per engineer, because why wouldn't you use these subsidies for your own company. However, consumer plans aren't designed for commercial use, so Anthropic, OpenAI and other labs have introduced special subscriptions for engineering teams. These have a predictable monthly price, but are subject to usage limits (based on token usage, not dollar amounts). Engineers who hit these limits either stop until the limit resets or continue at API pricing, so these plans are harder to budget for than they seem.


In this article, let's look at some examples of which pricing models work in which scenarios, and how companies can effectively budget for AI usage. I'll also introduce you to Emdash, a coding agent orchestrator that gives engineering teams one place to see and control what each developer spends across Claude Code, Codex, and other agents.


## How much does Claude Code cost per developer?


Claude Code costs about[$13 per developer per active day and $150 to $250 per developer per month](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/costs) on average across enterprise deployments. Individual days can cost far more, but the large majority of users stay under $30 per active day.


To give you an idea of prices at heavy usage, I recorded some of my own usage statistics. Some stats about my last month of using Claude Code at Anthropic's list prices:


- $4,988 in total
- $178 on an average day
- $832 on the busiest day
- 278 sessions, with a median cost of $2.74 and a largest session of $1,547
- 43% of all spend in the five largest sessions


## What 30 engineers would cost per month


You can pay for Claude Code through individual subscriptions, seats on a Team plan, tokens through the Claude Console, or an Enterprise plan that charges for both seats and tokens.


At[current prices](https://claude.com/pricing) , cost for a team of 30 engineers would look like this:


Plan Cost 30 engineers/mo Usage limits


Personal (Pro, Max or Ultra, one per person) $20, $100 or $200 a month $600, $3,000 or $6,000 Work stops until the window resets, unless usage credits are on


Team, Standard seats $20 a seat billed annually, $25 monthly $600 Work stops until the window resets, unless usage credits are on


Team, Premium seats $100 a seat billed annually, $125 monthly $3,000 Work stops until the window resets, unless usage credits are on


Claude Console (API) Tokens at list price, no seat fee $4,500 to $7,500 at average use Billing continues until a spend limit stops it


Enterprise $20 a seat billed annually, plus all usage at API rates $5,100 to $8,100 at average use Billing continues until a spend limit stops it


*Team and Enterprise seat prices on claude.com/pricing, 6 November 2026*


On their own, subscriptions and API pricing each have a trade-off.


With team plans, you'll have usage limits, but get predictable pricing. API pricing is more expensive and less predictable, but you get unlimited usage.


You don't necessarily need to choose either/or, though. If your team is small enough for the Team plan (up to 150 people), use Team seats with usage credits on. Each engineer can first use their subsidized seat allowance, then continue at API rates once they reach usage limits (e.g. the 5-hour limit). This way, the first part of their work will be subsidized, and you can limit extra usage through spend controls. For engineers with average or heavier usage, this costs less than pure API pricing.


Premium seats break even early. At average daily use ($13/day), they match API costs after about 8 active days a month. Premium seats have[5x the usage of Standard seats](https://claude.com/pricing) , and you can use both types on a single plan. Combined with usage credits, they’re what I’d recommend for company usage. The 150-seat limit is the point where you’d move to Enterprise and lose the subsidy.


As a side note, Anthropic earns far more from API pricing than from subscriptions:[its IPO filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026067168/anthropicpbc-sx1.htm) shows $13.1 billion of usage-based revenue in the first half of 2026, 80% of the total, against $3.2 billion from subscriptions.


## Can a company use Pro, Max or Ultra subscriptions?


Pro, Max and Ultra use[consumer terms](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/consumer-terms) , but there are different consumer terms for EEA and Switzerland, and those say "Non-commercial use only". The other version of consumer terms we read doesn't say that. Your lawyer can clarify. Or use the Team plan instead.


Pro, Max, Ultra Team, Enterprise, API


[Terms](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance) Consumer Commercial


Can people share access? No Yes, with a company API key


[Trains on your code?](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/data-usage) Only if that person's setting is on No, by default


[How long your data is kept](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/data-usage) 5 years if training is on, 30 days if off 30 days


[Data processing agreement?](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/commercial-terms) No Yes


Company admin controls and spend limits? No Yes


Personal subscriptions aren’t designed for company use. If each engineer uses their own subscription, it’s also hard to enforce company policies. For organizational use, you’ll likely want admin controls, spend limits, or a list of approved MCP servers.


Anthropic’s Team and Enterprise plans cover much of this for Claude Code. But most engineering teams don’t use just one coding agent. Some engineers prefer Codex, others want to try open-source models for cheaper tasks.


Each provider then comes with its own admin console, its own spend limits and its own reports. I'll cover a better way to handle this at the end of this article.


## What one task costs on each model


I evaluated Claude Code on[Hono](https://github.com/honojs/hono) , an open source TypeScript web framework of about 83,000 lines of code. I asked all four current models to perform each of the following tasks twice, at the default effort:


- **Bug fix:** I intentionally broke Hono’s handling of a query key with no value, described the problem, and asked Claude Code to fix the bug and write a regression test.
- **Feature:** we asked Claude Code to add a feature to the CORS middleware, including tests.


These are very straightforward tasks, and they can give us an idea of expected cost for a simple bug fix:


Model Input / output per million tokens Cache read per million tokens Bug fix Feature


Haiku 5.5 $0.10 / $0.50 $0.01 $0.01 $0.01


Sonnet 5.5 $2 / $10 $0.10 $0.08 $0.10


Opus 5.5 $4 / $20 $0.20 $0.15 $0.20


Fable 5.1 $10 / $50 $0.25 $0.61 $0.64


This was a set of short tasks, so the prompts were relatively small, making Haiku 5.5 much, much less expensive than Fable. (Though note that[Haiku becomes five times as expensive when prompts exceed 100,000 tokens](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing) ; cache reads contribute to the token count, so a longer session with Haiku won't retain as much of a discount.)


Opus was roughly twice as expensive as Sonnet. Fable (which[defaults to high effort](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config) , unlike the other three) was about 3.5 times more expensive than Opus.


For short tasks like this, the cost isn't high, regardless of model. Doing 20 tasks like this in a day would have cost about $3.50 on Opus, which is well below the $13 average.


You can run the same check on your own tasks, because Claude Code reports the cost of every run:


```text
claude   -p   "Where does Hono define its default router? Answer in one sentence."   \
--model   sonnet   --output-format   json   \
|   jq   '{cost: .total_cost_usd, turns: .num_turns, cache_read: .usage.cache_read_input_tokens, cache_write: .usage.cache_creation_input_tokens, output: .usage.output_tokens}'
```


```text
{
"cost"  :   0.018204599999999998  ,
"turns"  :   2  ,
"cache_read"  :   28366  ,
"cache_write"  :   5580  ,
"output"  :   141
}
```


This can be useful to get a cost estimation for real workloads in your organization and help you budget for the future.


## Why Claude Code sessions can get expensive


Claude’s replies (output tokens) were only 12% of my list-price total. Almost all of the rest went to the cache:


Claude Code[sends the whole conversation again on every request](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching) . It writes new content to the cache at a higher rate, then reads it back at a much lower rate on later requests.


**Longer conversations cost more per request.** On Opus 5.5, every request in a 500,000-token conversation costs $0.10 in cache reads alone, before Claude writes a single word. You might expect starting a fresh session for each task to help, but it really doesn't: starting over means paying to rebuild the cache each time.[Clearing helps](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/costs) mainly when a conversation has grown large and the next task doesn’t need it.


**Pausing a conversation is the expensive part.** The cache expires after five minutes on the API or with usage credits, and after an hour within a subscription’s usage. Once it expires, the next message needs to rebuild the cache from scratch. We sent the same one-word message to a mid-sized session twice. Sent right away, it cost $0.004. If we let the cache expire, it cost $0.093, which is 21 times as much for the same reply.


The longer the conversation, the larger the cost difference:


For API users who often step away from long sessions, an admin can extend the cache to one hour by setting` promptCacheTtl` to` 1h` . Writing to the cache then costs[more](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing) ($8 instead of $5 per million tokens on Opus 5.5), so it’s only worth it for people who regularly leave sessions idle.


## How do you limit Claude Code spend per developer?


Every way of purchasing Claude Code lets you set per-developer limits, but the controls are in different places:


You use See total spend Set a limit See spend per developer


Team or Enterprise Analytics page Organization settings > Usage CSV export from Analytics


Claude Console (API) Cost page Workspaces page Claude Code page


Bedrock, Google Cloud, Foundry Your cloud's billing console Your cloud's budgets, or a gateway OpenTelemetry or a gateway


**Team and Enterprise plans**


Each developer first uses their seat’s allowance. If an admin enables usage credits, they continue at API rates after that, up to the spend limit you set on those credits:


Enterprise plans also offer group limits and pooled budgets (in beta). Be careful here: a member with no individual limit and no group limit has no limit at all. A safe default is a limit per group, with an organization-wide limit as a backstop.


**Claude Console (API)**


Per-developer limits only work if each developer has their own API key. Developers get one automatically when they sign in to Claude Code with their own Console account. That’s the only workspace that supports per-user monthly spend limits, the Default Workspace doesn’t.


The Claude Code page then shows spend per member. In our example organization, everyone shares a single API key, so sessions and spend are not separated by developer in these charts:


To see what drives cost the most, the Cost page breaks spend down by workspace, API key and model:


*The Console’s Cost page, grouped by model*


As a backstop, set an organization-wide limit under Billing. It sends email alerts as spend gets close:


If you're using Bedrock, Google Cloud or Foundry, a[Claude apps gateway](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-apps-gateway-spend-limits) gives you per-developer limits by day, week or month. It blocks user requests above their limit, and warns the user at 75% and 95%.[OpenTelemetry](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage) works on every setup and streams per-user tokens and cost into your own monitoring.


## What if you want spend limits for multiple providers?


All of the controls above only cover Claude. If your engineers also use Codex, you need a second budget in a second admin console, with its own reports.


For example, ChatGPT Business charges[$20 per user per month billed annually, or $25 monthly](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/pricing) , and sets[monthly credit limits by seat type, with per-user overrides](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001155-managing-credits-and-spend-controls-in-chatgpt-business) , in OpenAI’s Admin Console. So a $500 limit on Claude and a $500 limit on Codex means $1,000 for that developer, and neither console shows the total. If you wanted to allow access to open-source models or another third agent, you'd need a third console.

## A general guideline about clever Claude usage


- If your team uses Claude daily, I'd recommend Premium Team seats with usage credits on
- Sonnet was half the cost of Opus on our small jobs, with little drop in quality. It might make sense to adjust your default model.
- Check the biggest sessions every month. Five sessions were 43% of my list-price total.
- Do a small pilot to see real spend before you buy for the whole team.
